title: Product Standardisation & Compliance
subtitle: Make your product the same every time, prove it on paper, and get ready for bigger buyers.
description: An advanced, hands-on course for women who already make and sell a product. You write a measured specification with tolerances, standard operating procedures and honest labels, check pack weights properly, count the cost of poor quality, train others to your standard and run your own internal audit and 90-day plan.
outcomes: Write a product specification in grams with tolerances, versions and a change log
Write and test one-page SOPs with checkpoints and safety steps
Check a label against the Codex labelling items and verify pack weights on a checked scale
Calculate your monthly cost of quality and the payback of a compliance spend
Prepare a buyer document pack and train helpers to a measured sign-off standard
Run an internal audit and write a 90-day plan for your top compliance gap
audience: Producers of food, cosmetics, crafts or garments who sell regularly and want to supply shops, hotels, distributors or other larger buyers.
tools: Digital scale reading to 1 g and a certified test weight (for example 100 g)
Notebook or Google Sheets for records
Canva or a printer's template for label artwork
Your current product, label and any registration documents

modules.title: Foundations: Writing the Standard Your Product Must Meet
modules.overview: You turn a product that lives in your hands and memory into a written specification with measured quantities and tolerances. You score how ready you are for the buyer you want, and you learn change control, the habit that lets you improve the product without letting it drift.

lessons.title: From 'my way' to a written specification with tolerances
objectives: Explain the difference between a recipe, a specification and a standard
Convert cup, handful and spoon measures into grams using a kitchen scale
Set a sensible tolerance for each ingredient and for the finished pack
Name the four layers of rules your product may have to meet in Nigeria

blocks.text: A buyer who has never met you cannot taste your care or watch your hands. What she can check is whether every pack is the same as the last one, and whether you can show on paper what "the same" means. That written description is your **product specification**, often shortened to **spec**. When you make every batch to it, and check that you did, your product becomes **standardised**.

Three words are easy to mix up, so fix them now. A **recipe or formula** lists what goes in and how much. A **specification** goes further: it adds the process steps, the conditions (time, heat, order), the packaging and a description of the finished product, with numbers wherever possible. A **standard** is a document that a group agrees everyone must meet, such as a Nigerian Industrial Standard published by the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON), or a buyer's own requirements. Your spec is your house standard.

blocks.name: scales
blocks.caption: Standardising starts with replacing cups and handfuls with weights you can repeat.

blocks.text: Why cups and handfuls fail

A cup of ground pepper packed down holds more than a cup poured loosely. A heaped spoon of salt changes with whoever is holding the spoon. Volume measures also change with how fine the grind is and how damp the ingredient is. **Weight does not care who is measuring.** A digital kitchen scale that reads to 1 gram costs far less than one rejected order, and it is the single most useful tool in this course.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a yaji recipe into grams
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Kaduna sells suya spice (yaji) in 100 g pouches. Her recipe was "4 cups groundnut powder, 2 cups pepper, ginger, garlic, onion powder and 2 heaped spoons of salt". Customers said some packs were too salty.
steps: She weighs each ingredient three times as she normally measures it. Her cup of groundnut powder averages 150 g, so 4 cups is 600 g. Her cup of pepper averages 100 g, so 2 cups is 200 g.
Her two heaped spoons of salt weigh 46 g, 55 g and 49 g on three tries. The average is (46 + 55 + 49) / 3 = 50 g, but the spread is 55 minus 46 = 9 g. That spread is why some packs tasted saltier.
She weighs the other ingredients the same way: ginger 80 g, garlic 40 g, onion powder 30 g.
She adds up the batch: 600 + 200 + 80 + 40 + 50 + 30 = 1,000 g. A 1 kg batch is easy to scale: a 3 kg batch is simply every number times 3.
She writes the formula in grams with a tolerance of plus or minus 5 g per ingredient for a 1 kg batch, and plus or minus 2 g for salt, because salt affects taste most.
blocks.result: Hauwa's spec now says 1,000 g batch: groundnut powder 600 g, pepper 200 g, ginger 80 g, salt 50 g (plus or minus 2 g), garlic 40 g, onion powder 30 g. The salty-pack complaints stop because salt is no longer measured by spoon.

blocks.text: What a full specification contains

head: Section
What to write
Yaji example
rows: Product name, size, spec number, version, date
Each ingredient or material, grade, approved supplier
Roasted groundnut powder, no mould or rancid smell, from approved supplier
Quantity per batch in grams or millilitres, with tolerance
As in the worked example, per 1 kg batch
Steps in order, with time, heat or mixing conditions
Sieve, weigh, mix 5 minutes in a clean bowl, pack same day
Reddish brown, even grind, no lumps, 100 g net per pouch
Container, seal, label version, batch code format
Laminated zip pouch, label version L2, code HY-date-batch

blocks.text: Tolerances: how much difference is allowed

No two batches are identical to the gram. A **tolerance** is the honest allowed range, written as a target plus or minus an amount. Set tighter tolerances for things that change safety, taste or the label (salt, preservatives, net weight) and looser ones for things that matter less. If you cannot measure a quality with a number, describe it in words and keep a reference: a sealed **reference sample** from a batch you were happy with, a photo, or a colour card. When you are unsure, you compare against the reference, not your memory.

blocks.title: The four layers of rules
blocks.caption: Your house spec sits at the base and must satisfy every layer above it that applies to your product.

blocks.text: Read the pyramid from the top. **Laws and regulators** come first: in Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates food, cosmetics, drugs, chemicals and similar products, and SON is responsible for standards for many other products. **National standards** describe minimum quality for a product type and are available from SON. **Buyers** such as supermarkets or hotels may add their own rules. Your house spec is where you write down how you meet all of these, plus your own quality choices.

blocks.title: Write the real recipe first
blocks.text: Write the spec for the product you actually make today, not an ideal one. If you secretly add more pepper when customers complain, write that down too, then decide properly. A spec that does not match reality is worse than none, because people will trust it.

blocks.title: Food hygiene comes with the spec
blocks.text: For food, build the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food into your process steps: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials. For groundnut products, reject any nuts that look mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured.

takeaways: A spec is a recipe plus process, conditions, packaging and a finished-product description.
Weigh everything; cups and spoons vary with the person and the ingredient.
Every number needs a tolerance, tighter where taste, safety or the label depends on it.
Your house spec must satisfy regulators, national standards and buyers that apply to you.

activity.title: Weigh your real recipe
steps: Choose one product you sell most often.
Measure each ingredient or material the way you normally do, then weigh it on a digital scale. Repeat three times and record all three.
Work out the average for each and note the biggest spread.
Write a one-page spec using the six sections in the table, with a tolerance beside every quantity.
Keep one sealed reference sample from a batch you are proud of, labelled with the date.
activity.evidence: Your one-page spec (version 1.0) and a photo of the three-weighings record and reference sample.

lessons.title: Scoring your readiness for the buyer you want
objectives: Match the level of standardisation to your target sales channel
Score your current position on an eight-point readiness check
Rank gaps by buyer importance and current readiness
Check whether your capacity fits the order size before you commit

blocks.text: Standardisation has a cost in time and money, so do it in the order your market demands. A woman selling to neighbours on WhatsApp, a woman supplying a supermarket and a woman tendering for a hotel contract need different paperwork. The skill in this lesson is to see exactly which gaps stand between you and your next buyer, and to fix those first.
What different buyers usually check

head: Channel
What buyers commonly look for
rows: Consistent product, honest label, easy reorder
Registration where the law requires it, full label, batch code, barcode for some chains, steady supply
Written spec, samples that match deliveries, invoices, delivery on schedule, sometimes a supplier form
All of the above plus formal documentation, testing or certification for the product and destination

blocks.text: These are common patterns, not rules. Always ask the actual buyer for their supplier requirements in writing. Many supermarkets and hotels have a supplier form or onboarding checklist; asking for it early shows seriousness and saves you guessing.

blocks.name: informed-decision
blocks.caption: A readiness score turns a vague worry into a clear list of what to fix first.

blocks.text: The eight-point readiness check

Score each item 0, 1 or 2. **0** means it does not exist. **1** means it exists but is incomplete, out of date or only in your head. **2** means it is written, current and followed by everyone who makes the product.

items: Written specification with weights and tolerances
Templates, measures or tools that make the product repeatable
Approved materials and at least one backup supplier
Accurate, complete label or tag (and care label where relevant)
Batch or order records you could show a buyer
A finished-product check before anything is packed
Packaging that protects the product in transport
Capacity to supply the volume the buyer wants

blocks.title: Worked example: tote bags for a hotel gift shop
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Aba sews ankara tote bags. A hotel gift shop asks for 200 bags per quarter, all one size, each with a care label, delivered with an invoice.
steps: She scores herself: spec 1, templates 2, materials and backup supplier 1, label 0, records 0, finished check 1, packaging 1, capacity 1.
She checks capacity: 200 bags over a 13-week quarter is 200 / 13 = about 15.4 bags a week. She makes about 25 a week, so volume is possible, but only if her other orders leave room.
She ranks gaps by what the hotel cares about. Care labels and same size are stated requirements, so the label (0) and spec (1) are urgent. Records (0) matter for invoicing and repeat orders.
She plans: finish the spec with exact measurements this week, order care labels next, and start an order record book before the first delivery.
blocks.result: Instead of feeling "not ready", Chioma has three named gaps in priority order and knows the volume is within her capacity.

blocks.title: Where each gap belongs
axes: Importance to this buyer (low to high)
blocks.caption: Gaps that matter to the buyer and score low go to the top of your plan.

blocks.text: Place each of your eight items on the matrix. Top left, **fix first**: important to this buyer and weak today. Top right, **keep and show**: important and already strong, so put it in your pitch. Bottom left, **schedule later**: weak but not yet needed. Bottom right, **do not overinvest**: already fine and not important to this buyer, so stop polishing it.
Business model questions to answer honestly

items: Will this buyer pay on delivery, or after 30 or more days? Can your cash carry the materials until then?
Does the order price cover the extra costs of labels, records and inspection time?
If the buyer doubles the order, can you still meet your own spec, or will quality slip?
Is this buyer a step towards a bigger channel, or a one-off?

blocks.title: Score with a second person
blocks.text: Ask a trusted helper or another producer to score you as well. We all rate our own work kindly. Where your scores differ by more than 1 point, look again with fresh eyes.
Readiness is not the same as quality

A producer can make an excellent product and still score low on readiness, because readiness measures whether the quality is written down, repeatable and provable. The reverse also happens: neat paperwork around a product customers do not like. Keep both in view. Before you spend on documents, confirm that buyers in your target channel actually want the product, for example by a small trial sale or by asking the buyer for feedback on a sample. Then use the scorecard to make that good product dependable. Repeat the scorecard every three months; a rising score is a simple, honest measure of progress you can show a business adviser or lender.

blocks.title: Do not promise what you cannot show
blocks.text: If a buyer asks for registration, a test report or a certificate you do not have, say so and give a realistic date. Claiming a registration you do not hold is illegal and ends trust instantly when checked.

takeaways: Different channels need different levels of documentation; let your next buyer set the order of work.
Score eight readiness items 0, 1 or 2 to see your real position.
Fix gaps that are important to the buyer and weak today before anything else.
Check capacity and payment terms before saying yes to a bigger order.

activity.title: Your readiness scorecard
steps: Name one specific buyer or channel you want in the next six months.
Ask them, or find out, what they require from suppliers, and write it down.
Score yourself on the eight-point check, then ask someone else to score you.
Place each item on the importance and readiness matrix.
Write your top three gaps in priority order with one first action each.
activity.evidence: The completed scorecard with both sets of scores, your matrix sketch and your top three gaps.

lessons.title: Change control: improving the product without letting it drift
objectives: Explain why unplanned small changes destroy consistency
Run a side-by-side trial batch before changing the spec
Update the spec version, label and team training after an approved change
Recognise changes that may need a regulator's approval

blocks.text: Most products do not change in one big step. They **drift**: a little more of this because the new supplier's pepper is milder, a slightly bigger handle because the worker prefers it, a different jar because it was cheaper this month. After six months the product on the shelf no longer matches the sample the buyer approved. **Change control** is the simple discipline that stops drift: no change to the product, its materials or its package goes into production until it has been tested, approved and written into a new version of the spec.

blocks.name: split-testing
blocks.alt: Two versions being compared side by side
blocks.caption: Test the old and new versions side by side before you change the spec.

blocks.text: What counts as a change

items: A new supplier or grade of any material, even if it has the same name
Any change in quantity, process step, time or temperature
A new container, closure, pouch or label
A new machine or tool that does a step differently
A new person doing a critical step for the first time

blocks.title: The change control path
blocks.caption: Every change follows the same five steps before it reaches a customer.

blocks.text: Keep a **change log** at the back of your spec file: date, what changed, why, the trial result, who approved it, and the new version number. Use simple numbering. A small change moves 1.0 to 1.1. A big change, such as a new main ingredient, moves 1.1 to 2.0. Remove or clearly mark old copies of the spec so nobody works from the wrong one.

blocks.title: Worked example: a hotter pepper from a new supplier
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa's usual pepper seller in Kaduna runs out, and the new supplier's ground pepper is noticeably hotter. Her spec (version 1.0) uses 200 g pepper and 600 g groundnut powder per 1 kg batch.
steps: She writes the proposal: new pepper supplier, reduce pepper and increase groundnut powder to keep heat and weight the same.
She makes two small trial batches on the same day: one with the old pepper at 200 g per kg (the control), and one with the new pepper at 170 g per kg and groundnut powder at 630 g per kg.
She checks the new formula adds up: 630 + 170 + 80 + 40 + 50 + 30 = 1,000 g.
She asks 10 regular customers to taste both, unlabelled. 7 say they cannot tell the difference or prefer the new one.
She checks the label: ingredients by weight are still groundnut powder, pepper, ginger, salt, garlic, onion powder, so the order on the label does not change. Net weight stays 100 g.
She records the change as version 1.1, files the trial notes and shows her packer the new weights.
blocks.result: The product stays consistent for customers even though the raw material changed, and Hauwa has a dated record that explains why her spec says 170 g.

blocks.text: Changes that touch the label or the law

Some changes reach beyond your kitchen. If the order of ingredients by weight changes, the ingredient list on the label must change. If you add an ingredient that is a known allergen, such as groundnut, wheat, milk, egg or soy, it must be declared. If your product is registered with NAFDAC, check with NAFDAC before changing the formula, pack size or label of the registered product, because the registration relates to the product as it was approved. Treat this as a change control step, not an afterthought.

blocks.title: One change at a time
blocks.text: If you change the pepper and the mixing time together and the taste changes, you cannot know which caused it. Change one thing per trial whenever you can.
Leading the discipline

Your team will copy what you do. If you add "a little extra" when you are in a hurry, they will too. Say clearly that ideas for improvement are welcome, and that the way to use an idea is to bring it to you for a trial, not to try it on a customer's order. When a trial succeeds, give credit to the person who suggested it. That keeps creativity alive while the product stays the same.

Good change control also covers your packaging suppliers. If the printer changes the label paper, or the jar seller offers a different lid, ask for a sample first and test it with your product: does the label stay on when the pouch is handled with oily fingers, does the lid seal without leaking when the jar lies on its side for a day? A packaging change that fails in a customer's bag costs far more than the small saving that tempted you. Record packaging trials in the same change log as formula changes, so the history of the whole product sits in one place.

blocks.title: Keep the old reference sample
blocks.text: When you approve a new version, keep one sealed sample of the last batch of the old version as well. If a buyer later says "this is different", you can compare honestly.

takeaways: Drift is many small unrecorded changes; change control stops it.
Test a change side by side with the current product before approving it.
Every approved change gets a new version number, a log entry and retraining.
Check whether a change affects the label, allergens or a NAFDAC registration.

activity.title: Start your change log
steps: Add a change log page to your spec with columns: date, change, reason, trial result, approved by, new version.
List any changes you have made in the past six months that were never written down.
Pick one change you want to make next and write the proposal.
Plan a side-by-side trial with a control batch and decide how you will judge it (for example, a blind tasting by 10 customers or measuring size).
activity.evidence: Your change log page and the written trial plan for one proposed change.

quiz.q: Hauwa's two heaped spoons of salt weighed 46 g, 55 g and 49 g. What is the best fix?
options: Use a bigger spoon so the heap matters less
Weigh salt on a digital scale with a tight tolerance such as 50 g plus or minus 2 g
Ask one person to always do the spoon measuring
Reduce salt so variation does not matter
quiz.explain: Weight is repeatable whoever measures. A tight tolerance on salt protects taste, which customers notice first.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in a specification but not in a simple recipe?
options: A description of the finished product with tolerances and the label version
quiz.explain: A spec adds process conditions, finished-product checks, packaging and labelling to the recipe.

quiz.q: Chioma scores 7 out of 16 on the readiness check. Her label scores 0 and the hotel requires care labels. Where does the label go on the matrix?
quiz.explain: It is important to this buyer and weak today, so it is a fix-first gap.

quiz.q: A buyer wants 200 bags in a 13-week quarter. About how many bags a week is that?
A worker suggests a longer mixing time she thinks gives a better texture. What should happen next?
options: She uses it on the next customer order to see
Thank her, write the proposal and run a side-by-side trial before changing the spec
Reject it, because the spec must never change
Accept it immediately because she knows the work well
quiz.explain: Change control welcomes ideas but tests them first, then updates the spec version and retrains everyone.

quiz.q: Hauwa's new formula moves groundnut powder to 630 g and pepper to 170 g. What must she also check?
options: That the batch still totals 1,000 g and the label ingredient order is still correct
Nothing else, a small change needs no record
That the pouch colour still matches
quiz.explain: Any formula change must still add up, and the ingredient list must stay in descending order by weight.

modules.title: Systems, Quality and Operations
modules.overview: You write standard operating procedures that work without you in the room, check that every label tells the truth and every pack holds what it says, and put a naira figure on the cost of poor quality so you can decide what to fix first.

lessons.title: Writing SOPs that work when you are not in the room
objectives: Describe the parts of a one-page standard operating procedure (SOP)
Write numbered steps with built-in checkpoints and records
Include the correct safety precautions for heat and hot oil
Test an SOP by having someone else follow it

blocks.text: Your specification says **what** the product must be. A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** says **how** to do one task so that it comes out right every time, whoever does it. A small business usually needs only a handful: receiving materials, making a batch, filling and sealing, labelling and coding, cleaning, and final inspection. Each one should fit on a single page that can be stuck on the wall or saved as a photo on a worker's phone.

blocks.name: task-list
blocks.alt: A woman ticking off a task list
blocks.caption: A good SOP is a short list of steps anyone can follow and tick off.

blocks.title: Parts of a one-page SOP
blocks.caption: If any of these six parts is missing, the SOP will be followed differently by different people.

blocks.text: Rules for writing steps

items: Start each step with an action verb: weigh, pour, wipe, seal, check, record.
Put one action in each step. "Fill and cap and label" is three steps.
Use numbers, not feelings: "102 g on the scale", not "fill well".
Mark **checkpoints** where the worker must stop and check before going on, and say what to do if the check fails.
Say which record to fill in and when, so the paperwork is part of the job, not an extra.
Use the words your workers use. If everyone calls the double boiler "the pot inside pot", write both.

blocks.title: Worked example: SOP for filling hair pomade jars
blocks.context: For example, Funmi in Ibadan makes an oil-based hair pomade in 100 g jars. Two helpers fill jars, and the jar weights vary. She writes SOP-03, version 1.0, using her own house rule of a 102 g fill target so that no jar falls below the 100 g on the label.
steps: Purpose: fill, cap and code 100 g jars from one melted batch. Use for every batch.

Materials and tools: clean dry jars and lids, digital scale reading to 1 g, jug with spout, clean cloth, batch code stamp, batch record sheet. Safety: heat-resistant gloves, long sleeves, lid for the pot within reach.
Step 1: Check the scale with the 100 g test weight. It must read 100 g. If not, stop and tell Funmi.
Step 2: Place an empty jar on the scale and press tare so it reads 0 g.
Step 3: Pour the melted pomade until the scale reads 102 g. Acceptable range: 101 g to 104 g.
Step 4: Checkpoint: weigh every 10th jar again after it sets a little. If any jar is below 101 g, top it up and tell Funmi.
Step 5: Wipe the rim, close the lid, and stamp the batch code on the base.
Step 6: Leave jars upright to set fully before packing. Record the number of jars filled and any rejects on the batch sheet.
blocks.result: Both helpers now fill to the same weight, every 10th jar is checked, and the batch sheet shows how many jars each batch gave. Funmi can travel for a day and the work still comes out the same.

blocks.title: Hot oil and wax safety
blocks.text: Melt oils and waxes in a double boiler or on low heat, never leave the pot unattended, and keep children and pets out of the work area. Wear heat-resistant gloves and long sleeves. If oil catches fire, turn off the heat and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket. Never pour water on burning oil, it makes the fire spread violently. Cool a burn under clean running water and seek medical help for serious burns.
The newcomer test

An SOP is only finished when someone who has never done the task can follow it and get the right result. Give the page to a helper or family member, say nothing, and watch. Every time they hesitate, ask a question or do something you did not expect, the SOP needs a clearer step. Rewrite, then test again. Two rounds usually catch most gaps.
Where SOPs live

Keep a master copy in a folder (paper or a shared Google Drive folder) with a simple index: SOP number, title, version, date. Put a laminated or plastic-sleeved copy at the place where the work is done. When a version changes through change control, collect and destroy the old copy at the workstation the same day. Two different versions on the wall is how mistakes start.

head: SOP number
Task
Record it creates
rows: Making a batch to the spec
Cleaning and sanitising tools and jars

blocks.title: Use photos for steps that are hard to describe
blocks.text: A clear phone photo of a correctly sealed jar or a properly attached handle is often better than a paragraph. Add it to the SOP with a one-line caption such as "Correct: no oil on rim".

takeaways: A spec says what the product is; an SOP says how to do one task the same way every time.
One action per step, numbers instead of feelings, checkpoints with clear actions if they fail.
Safety precautions belong inside the SOP, not in a separate document nobody reads.
An SOP is finished only when a newcomer can follow it without help.

activity.title: Write and test one SOP
steps: Choose the task where results vary most between people.
Write a one-page SOP with all six parts from the checklist diagram.
Include at least one checkpoint and the record to fill in.
Give it to someone who has never done the task, watch silently and note every hesitation.
Rewrite and save as version 1.1 with the date.
activity.evidence: Both versions of your SOP and your notes from the newcomer test.

lessons.title: True labels and true weights: checking what the pack promises
objectives: Check a food label against the internationally used Codex labelling items
Verify a scale with a test weight before checking pack weights
Sample and weigh packs, calculate the average and spot underweight packs
Decide what to do when a batch fails a weight check

blocks.text: A label is a promise. It promises what is inside, how much, who made it and how long it stays good. Standardisation means the promise is checked, not hoped for. In this lesson you check two things on every batch: that the **label matches the spec**, and that the **pack holds at least what the label says**.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: Every word and number on your label should trace back to your spec and your records.

blocks.text: What a prepackaged food label must show

The **Codex General Standard for the Labelling of Prepackaged Foods**, agreed by FAO and WHO member countries, is the reference many national food rules build on. Its mandatory items are below. NAFDAC's own labelling rules for Nigeria apply to products sold here, so confirm the details with NAFDAC for your product, but this list is the right starting point for any food label check.

head: Label item
What Codex requires
Check against
rows: A name that shows what the food truly is
All ingredients in descending order of ingoing weight
Declared in metric units: weight for solids, volume for liquids
A code that identifies the producer and the batch
Best before date; storage conditions if the date depends on them

blocks.text: Codex also sets how the date is written: day and month for products that last up to three months, month and year for longer ones. The date must come from evidence, such as a shelf-life test you recorded, not from a guess or a competitor's label. Known allergens such as groundnut, milk, egg, wheat and soy should be easy to see on the label, because for some people they are dangerous.

blocks.title: Never print a number you do not hold
blocks.text: Only print a NAFDAC registration number that NAFDAC has issued for that exact product. Words like "NAFDAC approved" or "SON certified" on a product that is not registered or certified are false claims and can lead to seizure and prosecution.
Step one: check the scale

A weight check is only as good as the scale. Before each session, place a known **test weight** (a certified 100 g or 500 g weight, bought from a scale supplier) on the scale. If the reading is off, the scale must be re-zeroed, recalibrated using the maker's instructions, or replaced. Never use a product pack as a test weight; its true weight is exactly what you are trying to find out.
Step two: sample and weigh

For a small batch, weigh 10 packs picked from the start, middle and end of filling, not the 10 nearest your hand. Write down every weight, then calculate the **average** (add them and divide by 10) and find the **lowest** pack. Many producers use two house rules: the average must be at least the declared weight, and no single pack may fall below a set lower limit. Official tolerances for net quantity are set by law, so ask the regulator what applies to your product and make your house rules at least as strict.

blocks.title: Worked example: a scale that reads 1 g high
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa checks a batch of 100 g yaji pouches. Her house rules: average at least 100.0 g, no pouch below 98.0 g. She weighs 10 pouches before checking her scale: 101.2, 100.4, 99.1, 102.0, 100.8, 98.6, 101.5, 100.9, 99.7 and 101.0 g.
steps: She adds them: 1,005.2 g. Average = 1,005.2 / 10 = 100.52 g. Lowest = 98.6 g. Both rules seem to pass.
Then she places her 100 g test weight on the scale. It reads 101 g. The scale reads 1 g too high.
She subtracts 1 g from every reading. The true average is 100.52 minus 1 = 99.52 g, and the lowest pouch is really 97.6 g.
Result against her rules: average 99.52 g is below 100.0 g (fail), and one pouch at 97.6 g is below 98.0 g (fail).
She holds the batch, recalibrates the scale, reweighs and tops up every pouch that is below 100 g, then raises her fill target to 101 g so the average sits safely above 100 g.
She records the problem, the fix and the new target on the batch sheet and updates SOP-03.
blocks.result: Without the test weight, Hauwa would have released an underweight batch while her records said it passed. Checking the scale first turned a hidden failure into a recorded correction.

blocks.title: The weight-check cycle
blocks.caption: Run the cycle every batch; the record is your proof of honest quantity.

blocks.text: Non-food products

The same thinking applies beyond food. A cosmetic jar should state its contents honestly and list ingredients. A garment or bag should carry fibre content and care instructions; the international care symbols use a washtub for washing, a triangle for bleaching, a square for drying, an iron for ironing and a circle for professional cleaning. Whatever the product, every claim on the label, including "handmade", "100% cotton" or "natural", must be something you can prove from your spec and supplier records.

takeaways: Check the label against the spec: name, ingredients by weight, net contents, address, batch code, date.
Verify the scale with a test weight before trusting any weight check.
Sample across the batch, record every weight, and check both the average and the lowest pack.
A failed check means hold, correct, record and adjust the process, not just repack quietly.

activity.title: Label audit and weight check
steps: Take one of your current labels and tick each Codex item in the table, noting anything missing or unprovable.
Check that the ingredient order matches your spec weights, heaviest first.
Verify your scale with a test weight and record the reading.
Weigh 10 packs from across one batch and calculate the average and lowest weight.
Write the result against your house rules and the action you took.
activity.evidence: Your marked-up label, the scale check reading and the 10-pack weight sheet with calculations.

lessons.title: The cost of quality: what standardisation saves and costs
objectives: Sort quality costs into prevention, checking and failure costs
Calculate monthly failure costs from rework, scrap and returns
Compare total quality cost before and after standardising
Work out how many sales a one-off compliance cost must unlock

blocks.text: Standardisation is not free: labels, templates, test weights and inspection time all cost money. But poor quality also costs money, it is just hidden in thread used twice, materials thrown away and refunds. Quality managers call the total of these the **cost of quality**. When you add it up honestly, you usually find that spending a little on prevention saves a lot on failures.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person working with a calculator
blocks.caption: Putting naira figures on rework and returns shows what standardising is really worth.

head: Type
What it includes
Tote bag examples
rows: Cutting templates, written spec, training time
Finding faults before the customer does
Final inspection time, measuring tape, test weights
Rework of crooked handles, scrapped bags
Refunds, replacement bags, lost repeat orders

blocks.title: Worked example: Chioma's monthly cost of quality
blocks.context: For example, Chioma makes about 200 ankara tote bags a month and sells them at about 8,000 naira each (approximate, illustrative figures). Before standardising, sizes vary because she cuts by eye.
steps: Before: 15% need rework, which is 30 bags. Each rework costs about 700 naira in labour and thread: 30 x 700 = 21,000 naira.
5% are scrapped, which is 10 bags. Each scrapped bag lost about 3,500 naira of material and labour: 10 x 3,500 = 35,000 naira.
4 bags a month come back for refund at 8,000 naira: 4 x 8,000 = 32,000 naira.
Failure cost before = 21,000 + 35,000 + 32,000 = 88,000 naira a month, with almost no prevention spending.

After: she buys cutting templates for about 45,000 naira, spread over 6 months = 7,500 naira a month. Inspection takes 10 hours a month at 1,000 naira an hour = 10,000 naira. Care labels cost about 60 naira x 200 = 12,000 naira. Prevention and checking = 7,500 + 10,000 + 12,000 = 29,500 naira.
Failures fall to 4% rework (8 bags x 700 = 5,600), 1% scrap (2 bags x 3,500 = 7,000) and 1 refund (8,000): 5,600 + 7,000 + 8,000 = 20,600 naira.
Total after = 29,500 + 20,600 = 50,100 naira. Saving = 88,000 minus 50,100 = 37,900 naira a month.
blocks.result: Quality cost per bag falls from 88,000 / 200 = 440 naira to 50,100 / 200 = about 251 naira, and fewer unhappy customers means more repeat orders on top.

blocks.title: Before and after standardising
blocks.caption: Moving spending from failures to prevention lowers the total and protects the brand.

blocks.text: Pricing compliance into every unit

Ongoing costs such as labels, inspection time and record books belong in your unit cost every month, not only in the month you started. One-off costs such as templates, a test weight, a label redesign or a registration should be spread over the months or units they serve. Then you can judge a one-off cost with a simple **payback question**: how many extra sales must it unlock to pay for itself?

items: Write the one-off cost, for example a label redesign and new printing plates at about 60,000 naira (illustrative).
Write the profit you keep from each extra unit sold, for example 250 naira per yaji pouch.
Ask: is the new buyer likely to take at least 240 pouches within a reasonable time? If yes, the cost is justified. If not, delay it.

blocks.text: Capacity: checks take time

Inspection and records take real minutes. If final inspection takes 3 minutes a bag, 200 bags need 600 minutes, which is 10 hours a month. Put that time in your weekly plan. When an order is bigger than your capacity including checks, the honest answer is a later delivery date or a smaller first order, not skipping the checks.

blocks.title: Track it for three months
blocks.text: Keep a simple tally of reworks, scraps and returns for three months. The numbers will show you exactly which fault costs most, and that is where your next prevention spending should go.
Where to spend first

Look at your four types of cost together. If external failures are high, your first spending should usually be on checking, so that faulty units stop reaching customers while you work on the cause. Once fewer faults escape, move spending upstream into prevention: better templates, clearer SOPs, training and better materials. Prevention is cheaper in the long run because it stops the fault being made at all, while checking only finds it after the time and material are spent. The goal is not zero spending on checks, but a steady shift from paying for failures to paying for doing it right the first time.

blocks.title: Prices are examples
blocks.text: All naira figures in this lesson are approximate examples to show the method. Use your own receipts and current market prices.

takeaways: Cost of quality = prevention + checking + internal failure + external failure.
Failure costs are usually hidden; count rework, scrap and refunds in naira.
Spread one-off costs and test them with a payback calculation.
Plan inspection time into capacity instead of skipping checks when busy.

activity.title: Your cost of quality sheet
steps: List last month's reworks, scraps and returns, even if estimated, and put a naira cost on each.
List what you spend now on prevention and checking.
Add up the four types to get your monthly cost of quality.
Choose one prevention step and estimate how much failure cost it could remove.
Run the payback calculation for one one-off compliance cost you are considering.
activity.evidence: A one-page cost of quality sheet with your totals and one payback calculation.

quiz.q: Which SOP step is written best?
options: Fill the jars well and cap them
Pour until the scale reads 102 g (range 101 g to 104 g)
Fill, cap, wipe and label carefully
quiz.explain: One action, a number and a range. The others are vague or combine several actions.

quiz.q: A pot of oil catches fire while melting pomade base. What should the worker do?
options: Throw a cup of water on it
Turn off the heat and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket
Fan the flames down with a cloth
quiz.explain: Removing heat and oxygen puts it out. Water makes burning oil spread violently, and carrying a burning pot risks serious burns.

quiz.q: Hauwa's 10 pouches average 100.52 g on a scale that reads 100 g test weight as 101 g. What is the true average?
quiz.explain: The scale reads 1 g high, so subtract 1 g: 100.52 minus 1 = 99.52 g, which fails a 100 g average rule.

quiz.q: Which of these must the ingredient list follow under the Codex labelling standard?
options: Any order, as long as all are listed
quiz.explain: Codex requires ingredients in descending order of ingoing weight at manufacture.

quiz.q: A label redesign costs about 60,000 naira and each extra pouch sold gives 250 naira profit. How many extra pouches pay it back?
Refunds for faulty bags that customers bring back are which type of quality cost?
quiz.explain: Faults found by the customer are external failures, usually the most damaging because they also cost trust.

modules.title: Growth, People and Proof
modules.overview: You turn your standards into documents larger buyers can trust, train others until consistency no longer depends on you, and run your own internal audit to choose the one compliance gap that matters most for the next 90 days.

lessons.title: Answering buyer requirements: data sheets, supplier forms and samples
objectives: Build a one-page product data sheet a buyer can file
Calculate case configuration and carton weight correctly
Answer a supplier questionnaire honestly, including the gaps
Keep retained samples that match what you send buyers

blocks.text: When a supermarket, pharmacy chain or hotel considers a new supplier, a buyer usually has to fill in forms and convince a manager. Make her job easy. A clean **product data sheet**, honest answers on the **supplier form** and **samples that match your deliveries** tell her you are a producer who will not cause problems later. Your spec from Module 1 is the source for all of it; the data sheet is the outward-facing summary.

blocks.name: handshake-deal
blocks.alt: Two people shaking hands over a deal
blocks.caption: Clear documents make it easy for a buyer to say yes and to defend that choice to her manager.

blocks.text: What goes on a product data sheet

head: Field
Example for a 100 g hair pomade
rows: Funmi's Shea and Coconut Hair Pomade, 100 g
Full list as on the label; many cosmetic buyers prefer international INCI names, for example Butyrospermum Parkii Butter for shea butter
100 g in a screw-top jar with tamper seal
NAFDAC registration number if issued; barcode (GTIN) if the buyer needs one
From your own shelf-life evidence; store in a cool, dry place
24 jars per carton, carton dimensions and gross weight
How to read your batch code, so the buyer can trace complaints
Phone, email, address, normal delivery time after order

blocks.text: Barcodes for retail are issued through **GS1**, the global barcode organisation, which has a Nigerian office (GS1 Nigeria). A barcode identifies your product in the shop's system; it is not a quality approval. Ask the buyer whether they need one before you pay for it.

blocks.title: Worked example: case configuration and carton weight
blocks.context: For example, a cosmetics shop chain in Ibadan asks Funmi for case details. Each filled and capped jar weighs 160 g in total (100 g pomade plus jar and lid). She packs 24 jars per carton, and the empty carton with dividers weighs 300 g.
steps: She weighs one filled jar on her checked scale: 160 g.
Jars per carton: 24, arranged 6 by 4 in one layer with cardboard dividers.
Gross carton weight = 24 x 160 g + 300 g = 3,840 g + 300 g = 4,140 g, about 4.1 kg.
She measures the outer carton with a tape: length, width and height in centimetres, and adds them to the data sheet.
She checks an order of 10 cartons: 10 x 24 = 240 jars, and about 10 x 4.14 = 41.4 kg for the delivery van.
blocks.result: The buyer can now plan shelf space, storage and delivery from Funmi's data sheet without calling her, and the numbers come from real weighing.

blocks.text: Answering a supplier questionnaire

Supplier forms often ask about registration, hygiene practices, complaints handling, recalls and insurance. Answer every question truthfully. Where you are not there yet, write what you have and a date: "NAFDAC registration application in progress, expected by March" is acceptable to many buyers; a false "yes" found out later is not. Attach evidence where you can: a photo of your batch record, your label, your cleaning log.

blocks.title: Your buyer document pack
blocks.caption: Keep this pack ready as PDFs on your phone so you can send it the same day a buyer asks.

blocks.text: Samples and retained samples

The sample you send a buyer becomes the standard they judge every delivery against. Send samples from a normal production batch, not a specially perfected one, and note the batch code. From every batch you sell, keep a few units as **retained samples**, labelled with the batch code and stored as the product should be stored. If a customer complains, you open the retained sample from the same batch and see whether the fault was in production or happened later in transport or storage.

blocks.title: Use your standard as your pitch
blocks.text: Lead with proof: "Every jar is filled to at least 100 g, checked on a verified scale, and every batch is coded and recorded." A buyer hears many people say their product is good. Few can show how they know.
Know the national schemes

For many manufactured products, SON runs product certification against Nigerian Industrial Standards, including its MANCAP programme for products made in Nigeria. NAFDAC registration covers regulated products such as food and cosmetics. Which applies depends on your product, so ask the agency directly or use their official offices and websites, and never pay an agent who promises a certificate without an inspection.

Keep your data sheet in step with your spec. Give it the same version number and date, and update it through change control whenever the formula, pack or carton changes. Buyers often file the first data sheet you send and use it for years, so send a dated update whenever something on it changes, with a one-line note of what is different.

blocks.title: Protect your documents
blocks.text: Send buyers copies, not originals, and add a watermark such as "Copy for [buyer name] only" to registration certificates. This reduces the risk of your documents being misused by someone else.

takeaways: A product data sheet summarises your spec in the form buyers need.
Case configuration and weights must come from real measurement, with checked arithmetic.
Answer supplier forms honestly; a dated plan is better than a false yes.
Send normal-batch samples and keep retained samples from every batch.

activity.title: Build your buyer pack
steps: Create a one-page product data sheet with all eight fields for your main product.
Weigh a full unit and an empty carton, and calculate gross carton weight for your case size.
Collect the six documents in the checklist as phone PDFs or photos.
Start a retained sample box: three units from your next batch, labelled with the batch code.
activity.evidence: Your data sheet, the carton weight calculation and a photo of your retained sample box.

lessons.title: Training for consistency: skills matrix, sign-off and a stop rule
objectives: Build a skills matrix showing who can do which task to standard
Use a clear sign-off rule based on measured results
Introduce a no-blame stop rule for doubtful batches
Train people to keep records accurately and understand why

blocks.text: Standardisation is tested the first time someone else makes the product. If quality drops when you are away, the standard lives in you, not in the business. Training for consistency has three parts: show clearly, check with numbers before signing someone off, and make it safe for anyone to stop the work when something looks wrong.

blocks.name: teaching
blocks.alt: A woman teaching a small group
blocks.caption: Training is complete when results are measured, not when the explanation is over.

blocks.text: The skills matrix

A **skills matrix** is a simple grid: people down the side, tasks across the top, and a level in each box. It shows at a glance who can do what, who is still learning and where you have only one trained person, which is a risk if she is sick.

Levels: **0** not trained. **1** trained, works only under supervision. **2** signed off, works alone to standard. **3** can train others. In the grid above, only Chioma can do final inspection alone, so training Blessing to level 2 on inspection is a priority.

blocks.title: From learner to signed off
blocks.caption: Each stage is a step on the skills matrix, from level 0 up to level 2.

blocks.text: Sign off on numbers, not feelings

Decide a sign-off rule for each task before training starts, so it is fair and clear. For a production task, a common approach is a run of consecutive batches that meet the spec. Write it into the SOP so every learner knows the target.

blocks.title: Worked example: signing Amina off on handles
blocks.context: For example, Chioma's rule for handle attachment is: three batches of 10 bags in a row, each with no more than 1 bag needing rework, checked against the handle spec (length 60 cm plus or minus 1 cm, stitched 4 cm into the bag, double row).
steps: Amina's first four batches have 3, 1, 0 and 1 handles needing rework.
Batch 1: 3 out of 10 = 30% rework, which is above the rule, so the count restarts.
Batches 2, 3 and 4: 1, 0 and 1 out of 10, each within the rule. That is three in a row.
Over those three batches she made 30 bags with 2 reworks: 2 / 30 = about 6.7%.
Chioma signs and dates Amina's line on the matrix, moving her from level 1 to level 2, and notes a refresher check in three months.
blocks.result: Amina is signed off on evidence she can see herself, and Chioma has a dated record to show a buyer how she trains staff.

blocks.text: The stop rule

Write one clear sentence and say it often: **"If anything does not match the spec, stop, set it aside and tell me. You will never be blamed for stopping."** Examples: a material that smells or looks different, a scale that fails its test weight check, a label roll with the wrong batch format. Thank the person who stops a batch, even if it turns out fine. If people fear blame, they hide problems, and hidden problems reach customers.
Teaching records, not just skills

Records are the part of the job most likely to be skipped or filled in at the end of the day from memory. Explain why each record matters, in one line: "This weight sheet is our proof to the supermarket that every jar is full." Show a correctly completed sheet as the model. Check records daily at first, and correct gently but immediately: an entry made from memory is not evidence.

blocks.title: Train the safety steps first
blocks.text: Where the work involves hot oil, sharp cutting tools, sewing machines or cleaning chemicals, train and sign off the safety steps before the production steps. A learner should know where the lid, first aid box and exit are before she touches the pot.
Refresher checks and new tasks

Skills fade and habits slip, especially after a busy season. Plan a short refresher check for every signed-off person, for example every three months: watch her do the task once against the SOP and check the last few batch records she filled. If results have slipped, move her back to level 1 for that task until she meets the sign-off rule again, and treat it as normal, not as punishment. Whenever an SOP changes through change control, everyone signed off on that task needs a quick retraining on the new version, recorded on the matrix with the date. Aim to have at least two people at level 2 on every critical task, so that one person's illness or travel never stops production or lowers quality.

When you hire someone new, start her on tasks where mistakes are easy to catch, such as packing and labelling under supervision, before moving to tasks such as formula weighing where errors are harder to see in the finished product.

blocks.title: Use short video notes
blocks.text: Record a short phone video of a correct task (no faces needed) and share it in your staff WhatsApp group. Learners can watch it again before a shift, and it uses less data than a long explanation call.

takeaways: A skills matrix shows who can work alone to standard and where you depend on one person.
Agree sign-off rules in advance and base them on measured results.
A no-blame stop rule keeps problems visible and away from customers.
Teach the purpose of each record so it is filled in honestly, at the time.

activity.title: Your skills matrix
steps: List everyone who helps produce your product, including family and part-time helpers.
List four to six key tasks from your SOPs.
Fill in the 0 to 3 levels honestly.
Write a measurable sign-off rule for the task where you depend most on yourself.
Write your stop rule sentence and display it where the work happens.
activity.evidence: A photo of your skills matrix, your sign-off rule and your displayed stop rule.

lessons.title: Internal audit, gap analysis and your 90-day standardisation plan
objectives: Run a simple internal audit of your own standards and records
Turn audit findings into a scored gap list
Choose the single gap most limiting your growth
Write a 90-day plan with steps, owners, dates and a budget

blocks.text: An **internal audit** is you, or someone you trust, checking whether what your documents say is what actually happens. It is the habit behind quality systems such as ISO 9001, the international standard for quality management systems, which is built on principles like customer focus, a process approach and continual improvement. You do not need ISO certification to borrow the habit. A two-hour audit every quarter keeps your standards alive and gives you honest evidence for buyers.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a large checklist
blocks.caption: An internal audit compares what your papers say with what really happens.

blocks.text: How to run a two-hour audit

items: Pick one product and gather its spec, SOPs, label, last month's batch records and the skills matrix.
Watch one batch being made without helping. Note every place where practice differs from the SOP.
Pick three finished units at random and check them against the spec: weight, appearance, label, batch code.
Trace one batch backwards: from a sold unit's batch code to the batch record to the materials used. Note any break in the chain.
Score each audit area 0, 1 or 2 and write one sentence of evidence for each score.

blocks.title: Worked example: Funmi's quarterly audit
blocks.context: For example, Funmi audits her hair pomade across eight areas, scoring each 0 (missing), 1 (partly working) or 2 (working with evidence).
steps: Spec current and followed: 2. Batch watched matched the spec.
SOPs at the workstation and current: 1. The filling SOP on the wall was still version 1.0.
Scale checked before use: 2. Test weight log signed every day.
Label correct and complete: 1. Batch code is stamped on the base but the label has no best before date.
Batch records complete: 1. Two batches last month have no fill weights recorded.
Traceability: 0. A jar from a customer complaint could not be matched to its materials because supplier batch numbers were not written down.
Retained samples: 0. None kept.
Training and sign-off: 2. Matrix up to date.
blocks.result: Funmi's weakest areas are traceability and retained samples (both 0). Because a pharmacy chain she is targeting asks how she handles complaints and recalls, she chooses traceability as her top 90-day priority.

blocks.text: From gap list to one priority

Write every score below 2 as a gap. Then ask three questions of each: Does a buyer I want require it? Could it harm a customer if it fails? How much does it cost to close? Choose **one** top priority, the gap that scores high on the first two questions. Quick fixes that cost almost nothing, like replacing an old SOP on the wall, should be done this week and not wait for the plan.

blocks.title: A 90-day plan in three blocks
blocks.caption: Set up the system, use it on real batches, then audit it and turn it into evidence.

head: Days
Action
Owner
Budget (approximate)
rows: Add supplier name and supplier batch number columns to the goods-in log and batch record
About 2,000 naira for a new record book
Retrain both helpers on the new columns; add a retained sample shelf
About 5,000 naira for a shelf and labels
Add best before date to the label after reviewing shelf-life records
Label reprint cost, from printer quote
Record every batch fully; keep 3 retained jars per batch
Mock recall: pick a batch code and trace it to materials and customers within 2 hours
Repeat the internal audit; update the buyer pack with the trace test result

blocks.text: A **mock recall** is a practice run. You pretend a batch is faulty and see how quickly you can find which materials went into it and who bought it. If you cannot do it in a few hours, your records need work. Doing this on purpose, before a real complaint, is one of the strongest pieces of evidence you can show a buyer.

blocks.title: Measure success with a number
blocks.text: Set one measurable target for the 90 days, such as "traceability audit score from 0 to 2" or "mock recall completed in under 2 hours". A number tells you whether the plan worked.

Ask someone else to audit you at least once a year: a fellow producer, a cooperative member or a business adviser. Offer to audit her business in return. Fresh eyes notice what you have stopped seeing, and practising on each other prepares you both for the day a buyer or a regulator's inspector visits.

blocks.title: Your capstone
blocks.text: Your final project brings together your specification sheet, an accurate label, and this gap analysis and 90-day plan. The work you did in each lesson is the raw material.

takeaways: An internal audit checks that practice matches documents, using evidence.
Score each area, list every gap, then choose one priority that buyers need and that protects customers.
Do near-free fixes immediately; plan the bigger gap over 90 days.
A mock recall is strong proof that your records really work.

activity.title: Audit and plan
steps: Run the two-hour audit on your main product and score the eight areas.
List all gaps and do any near-free fixes this week.
Choose one priority gap using the three questions.
Write a 90-day plan table with actions, owners, dates and approximate budget.
Set one measurable target and a date for your next audit.
activity.evidence: Your scored audit sheet, gap list and 90-day plan table.

quiz.q: A filled jar weighs 160 g and an empty carton 300 g. What is the gross weight of a 24-jar carton?
quiz.explain: 24 x 160 = 3,840 g, plus 300 g for the carton = 4,140 g.

quiz.q: A supplier form asks if your product is NAFDAC registered. Your application is in progress. What should you write?
options: Yes, to avoid losing the buyer
In progress, with the expected date and what you already have
quiz.explain: Honest answers with a realistic date keep trust; a false yes is illegal and destroys the relationship when checked.

quiz.q: Amina's handle rework counts are 3, 1, 0, 1 for four batches of 10. The rule is three batches in a row with no more than 1. Is she signed off?
quiz.explain: Batches 2, 3 and 4 are three consecutive batches with 1 or fewer reworks, so she meets the rule after batch 4.

quiz.q: A helper notices the pomade base smells different from usual. What should your stop rule make her do?
options: Use it and mention it later
Add fragrance to cover the smell
Stop, set it aside and tell the owner without fear of blame
quiz.explain: The stop rule keeps doubtful materials out of production and makes problems visible.

quiz.q: Funmi could not match a complaint jar to its materials. Which audit area scored 0?
quiz.explain: Tracing a sold unit back to its materials is traceability; missing supplier batch numbers broke the chain.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of keeping retained samples from each batch?
options: To give free samples to new customers
To compare against complaints and see if a fault came from production or later handling
To sell later at a discount
quiz.explain: Retained samples let you check the same batch the complaint came from.

finalQuiz.q: Which document describes how to do one task the same way every time, whoever does it?
finalQuiz.explain: The spec says what the product must be; an SOP says how to do one task.

finalQuiz.q: Your cup of groundnut powder weighs 150 g on average. How much is 4 cups?
Which gap should go first in your plan?
options: Strong today and not important to your target buyer
Weak today and required by your target buyer
Weak today and not needed by any buyer yet
Strong today and important to the buyer
finalQuiz.explain: Weak and important gaps are fix-first; strong and important items are what you show in your pitch.

finalQuiz.q: A new pepper supplier sends hotter pepper. What is the correct first step?
options: Keep the old recipe and hope customers do not notice
Write the proposed change and run a side-by-side trial against the current product
Reduce the pepper on the next order and see
finalQuiz.explain: Change control: propose, trial, compare, approve, then update the spec, label if needed and training.

finalQuiz.q: Under the Codex labelling standard, how is net contents declared for a solid food?
finalQuiz.explain: Net contents must be in metric units: weight for solids, volume for liquids.

finalQuiz.q: Before weighing 10 packs, what should you check?
options: The scale, using a certified test weight
finalQuiz.explain: If the scale is wrong, every weight you record is wrong, as Hauwa's 1 g high scale showed.

finalQuiz.q: Ten packs weigh a total of 995 g on a checked scale. The house rule says the average must be at least 100 g. What is the result?
finalQuiz.explain: 995 / 10 = 99.5 g, which is below 100 g, so the batch fails and must be corrected.

finalQuiz.q: Rework fell from 30 bags to 8 bags a month at 700 naira each. How much does the business save on rework monthly?

options: Cutting templates that make every bag the same size
finalQuiz.explain: Prevention stops faults before they happen; the others are failure costs.

finalQuiz.q: Why send a buyer samples from a normal production batch?
options: The sample becomes the standard every delivery is judged against
It avoids needing a data sheet
finalQuiz.explain: A specially perfected sample sets a standard your normal deliveries may not meet.

finalQuiz.q: On a 0 to 3 skills matrix, what does level 2 mean?
options: Signed off to work alone to standard
finalQuiz.explain: Level 2 is signed off on measured results and works alone to the standard.

finalQuiz.q: What does a mock recall test?
options: How fast you can sell a batch
Whether your records let you trace a batch to its materials and customers quickly
finalQuiz.explain: A mock recall checks traceability before a real complaint forces it.

capstone.title: Product Standardisation & Compliance Pack
capstone.brief: Produce a standardisation pack for one real product: a written specification sheet (materials, quantities with tolerances, process steps, finished-product standard), an accurate label checked against your spec, and an internal audit with a gap analysis naming your top compliance priority and a realistic 90-day plan to close it.
steps: Weigh your real recipe or measure your real pattern three times and write the specification sheet in grams or centimetres with tolerances, version number and change log.
Write and newcomer-test at least one SOP for the task where results vary most.
Design or correct your label so every item matches the spec, the ingredient or material order is right and no unproven claim or unissued number appears.
Verify your scale with a test weight and record a 10-unit weight or measurement check from one batch.
Run the two-hour internal audit, score eight areas and list every gap.
Choose your top priority gap and write a 90-day plan with actions, owners, dates, approximate budget and one measurable target.
evidence: Specification sheet with tolerances, version and change log
Final label artwork with a tick-list against the spec
Scale check reading and 10-unit check sheet with calculations
Scored internal audit sheet and gap list
90-day plan table with a measurable target

sources.title: FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius: General Standard for the Labelling of Prepackaged Foods
WHO: Five Keys to Safer Food Manual
NAFDAC: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME)
Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON): services including MANCAP and SONCAP
